newsitem.title: LEBANON: Ban on Lebanon TV and radio goes into effect.
newsitem.headline: Ban on Lebanon TV and radio goes into effect.

text.p: Dozens of private television and radio stations refrained on Wednesday from broadcasting news bulletins a day after the Lebanese government refused to license them.

The government ban -- and its order for most of them to close by the end of November -- caused a storm of protest among opposition politicians who said it was an attempt to curb press freedoms and to allow political chiefs to monopolise the media.

The cabinet of Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri licensed four major private television stations and 12 radio stations -- owned by political leaders or businessmen -- out of a mass of media outlets dominating air waves since the 1975-90 civil war.

The cabinet ordered all other stations to stop broadcasting news and political programmes as of Wednesday but it left the door open for granting more licenses if stations refiled complete applications to a government-appointed agency to restudy their situations by the end of November.

"If these institutions correct the mistakes in their files and lodge new applications...they might be granted licenses if there was still room (for them to go on air)," Information Minister Farid Makari said.
The government ordered the rest to close by the end of November.

"This authority which has not washed its hands from the massacres it carried out against democracy during parliamentary elections has rushed to commit a new massacre against media freedoms," the Lebanese Communist Party said in a statement issued in Beirut newspapers.
Five rounds of parliamentary elections were carried out on the five previous Sundays amid widespread accusations of fraud.

The government decision was also attacked by the pro-Iranian Hizbollah -- whose television and a radio station were not licensed but granted a special permission to operate "as long as Israel occupied Lebanese land".
They were permitted to broadcast news on the guerrilla campaign they lead to oust Israeli troops from a 15-km (nine miles)-wide south Lebanon occupation zone.
"The cabinet decision is a political one aiming at silencing the voice of the opposition through licensing television and radio stations which it can control," the militant group said in a statement.

The government licensed the following television stations: Future Television of Hariri, NBN, a station which Parliament Speaker Nabih Berri is reported to be setting up, MTV of the brother of Deputy Prime Minister Michel al-Murr and Lebanon's top private station LBCI.
It also licensed a radio station owned by Hariri, another one Berri is setting up, and a third owned by a group of Lebanese investors.
Estimates of the present number of television stations range between 38 and 57, plus 150 radio stations. Some were militia mouthpieces during the war but have turned commercial since.
Some 63 television and radio stations had lodged applications. State-run Tele Liban and Lebanon Radio are already licensed.
